title: Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss

concept.text: The innovation would combine reliable identification of people at meaningful risk with an intervention that prevents Alzheimer’s dementia before substantial, irreversible loss of everyday function. It would need to interrupt disease early enough, remain effective long enough, and avoid harms that outweigh the benefit of treating people who may still feel healthy. The goal is a durable clinical benefit, rather than a change in a laboratory or imaging measurement alone.

Preventing clinical dementia is distinct from preventing the first detectable Alzheimer-related pathology. The June 2026 prevention-trial perspective uses primary prevention for intervention before detectable amyloid pathology. NRL-09 is defined by the eventual clinical outcome: preserving cognition and daily function before major loss. Preventing pathology could be one route to that outcome, but neither preventing amyloid accumulation nor clearing existing plaques would, by itself, demonstrate that dementia has been prevented.

significance.text: If safe, accessible prevention worked reliably for most at-risk people, a substantial cause of neurological disability would become preventable. The direct benefit would be more years with preserved cognition, independence and daily function. The supplied perspective motivates early intervention through the burden of Alzheimer disease and the possibility of interrupting its pathological cascade before symptoms develop; it does not establish that this outcome is already achievable.

Conditional impact synthesis: Broadly effective prevention could also reduce caregiving demands and long-term care needs. Those downstream benefits would depend on how many people benefit, how long protection lasts, treatment and monitoring burdens, affordability, and access. A result confined to a narrowly selected inherited-disease population would not establish comparable population-wide impact.

The impact has important boundaries. Preventing Alzheimer’s dementia would not automatically prevent dementia from other causes, and preserving function before injury would not establish an ability to rebuild damaged tissue or recover abilities already lost. A delay in symptom onset could be clinically valuable, but its significance would depend on its duration; delay during a finite study cannot establish lifelong prevention.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the reliable combination of prediction and safe, durable clinical prevention. Presymptomatic risk identification already exists in some settings, particularly for people carrying mutations associated with dominantly inherited Alzheimer disease. The broader challenge is identifying people in the general population who are sufficiently likely to develop clinical disease, early enough for intervention to help. The perspective describes the substantial screening effort, cost and time required to recruit such populations.

A central biological uncertainty is whether the chosen intervention interrupts the processes that ultimately cause clinical deterioration. The perspective explicitly asks whether preventing or clearing larger amyloid plaques is sufficient to slow or stop long-term progression when an immunotherapy may not target amyloid seeds. Target engagement and plaque reduction therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable with preserved cognition or prevention of dementia.

Prevention also requires a workable treatment duration and safety profile for people without substantial impairment. Potentially prolonged or lifelong treatment raises questions about cumulative harms, sustained benefit and monitoring burden. Establishing the clinical outcome is itself difficult: the perspective explains that the long interval before clinical events makes maintaining a placebo comparison challenging and a clinical endpoint infeasible for its proposed platform, which instead uses biomarker outcomes.

current_state.text: The June 2026 perspective, “Primary prevention of Alzheimer disease in dominantly inherited Alzheimer network: a platform trial design,” documents active prevention research and describes planned or ongoing studies in inherited and sporadic Alzheimer disease. It is a trial-design perspective, not a completed demonstration of durable dementia prevention. The supplied review assessed its complete main-article HTML prose; figure images and supplementary documents were not inspected. Although the source index also lists a PDF, this record makes no claim of an additional assessment of that artifact.

That perspective reports preliminary evidence from an open-label gantenerumab extension involving asymptomatic people with dominantly inherited Alzheimer disease. Long-term treatment at doses associated with only partial amyloid-plaque removal may have substantially delayed first symptom onset. This is a reported preliminary finding in a rare inherited form of disease, rather than proof of durable prevention of clinical dementia in the general at-risk population. The underlying 2025 study report was not supplied, so its methods, effect estimates and uncertainties were not independently assessed in the review.

The earlier research describes lecanemab as producing less clinical decline and reduced amyloid markers, with adverse events, in an 18-month phase III trial of early symptomatic Alzheimer disease. Those details remain unverified within the supplied evidence: the retained PubMed copy contains only a cookie barrier, not the abstract or study text. The earlier assertion that the abstract was inspected therefore cannot be substantiated. This access limitation does not show that the reported findings are false, but the duration, trial phase, efficacy and harms cannot be presented here as verified results. Even as originally described, slowing decline after symptoms begin would not demonstrate presymptomatic prevention.

The DIAN-TU-002 platform described in the perspective uses biomarkers as its primary and key secondary outcomes because of the practical difficulty of waiting for clinical events. Such studies can test early biological effects and inform prevention strategies, but biomarker success alone would leave the central clinical question unresolved. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded search entries establishing whether subsequent results changed the picture by November 1, 2026; the dated June account should not be read as a verified account of all later developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: Large randomized trials beginning before substantial impairment should show a durable reduction in clinically meaningful Alzheimer’s dementia, accompanied by preserved daily function and acceptable long-term safety. The protocol should specify meaningful effect sizes, follow-up duration, dementia ascertainment and acceptable harm thresholds in advance. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established standards supplied by the reviewed paper.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trials demonstrate durable, safe dementia reduction preserving daily function

completion_criteria.text: Clinical outcomes would need to anchor the conclusion, with biomarker changes supporting interpretation of mechanism and treatment response. The perspective’s reliance on biomarker endpoints illustrates the feasibility problem: a practical early-stage platform can answer useful biological questions without completing the more demanding demonstration that dementia and functional loss have been prevented.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical outcomes demonstrate prevention of dementia and functional loss

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: Independent replication and sufficiently diverse study populations should establish who benefits, who does not, and how results differ between dominantly inherited and more common sporadic disease. Follow-up should distinguish sustained protection from a temporary postponement and examine whether benefit requires continued treatment. Finite trials would establish benefit across the populations and observation periods tested, rather than literal universality or lifelong protection.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes protection’s durability and scope across diverse populations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: Population-scale completion should also require a feasible route from risk identification to treatment and monitoring, with affordable access and an acceptable burden for people without symptoms. Strong efficacy in a specialized trial would establish a narrower achievement if screening costs, treatment harms or delivery requirements prevented broad use.
completion_criteria.label: Population-scale prevention is affordable and feasible for asymptomatic people

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-11, “Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function,” is the closest companion. NRL-09 seeks to preserve function before substantial irreversible loss; NRL-11 addresses established disease and recovery afterward. Their biology and treatments could overlap, but success in either would not establish the other. The supplied roster confirms NRL-11’s title and this broad distinction; its detailed specification was not supplied.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could enable a prevention strategy if that strategy required selective delivery. It is a general delivery capability, whereas NRL-09 requires evidence of clinical prevention. NRL-15, “Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases,” overlaps in disease-mechanism research, but a shared mechanism would need disease-specific validation before it could support an Alzheimer’s prevention claim.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-04, “Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories,” and NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” concern repair or preservation of particular neural substrates. NRL-09 could succeed by preventing damage without acquiring either capability. Conversely, repairing a memory trace or replacing tissue would not by itself establish control of the continuing Alzheimer disease process. These remain distinct innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved NRL-09’s identity and expanded its explanation around integrated risk identification, early intervention and durable clinical benefit.
change_log.reason: The review supports a coherent unmet capability while clarifying that presymptomatic identification already exists in some settings.

change_log.change: Separated clinical dementia prevention from prevention of detectable amyloid pathology and from biomarker response.
change_log.reason: The perspective’s primary-prevention terminology concerns an earlier pathological stage, and plaque changes do not alone establish clinical prevention.

change_log.change: Specified the preliminary inherited-disease evidence as an open-label gantenerumab extension reported by the June 2026 perspective.
change_log.reason: This preserves the useful finding while making its design, population, indirect sourcing and limited generalizability explicit.

change_log.change: Corrected the claimed lecanemab abstract inspection and retained the earlier trial description only as explicitly unverified supplied research.
change_log.reason: The retained PubMed artifact is a cookie barrier. Preserving the qualified quantitative account avoids treating inaccessible evidence as either verified or disproven.

change_log.change: Added biological uncertainties about amyloid seeds and plaques, treatment duration, screening burden and the feasibility of clinical endpoints.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why early biological activity has not yet established the proposed clinical capability.

change_log.change: Separated proposed completion requirements from the documented platform’s biomarker endpoints.
change_log.reason: Diversity, replication, clinical outcomes, safety and access are reasoned proposals for convincing completion, not established standards in the supplied source.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain related concepts, including NRL-11, without assuming their detailed specifications.
change_log.reason: The roster permits title-level comparison but does not establish the full scope of those entries.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access, inspection and freshness limitations in the relevant current-state paragraphs.
change_log.reason: The review assessed article prose, did not inspect figures or supplements, and did not establish completeness through the November as-of date.

unresolved_issues: The lecanemab paper’s identity and reported 18-month phase III efficacy and harms cannot be verified from the retained cookie-barrier artifact. The review’s recommendation to remove those details entirely was not adopted because the task requests preservation of unresolved quantitative detail with explicit qualification; they remain attributed to the earlier research rather than asserted as verified findings.
The underlying 2025 gantenerumab extension report was not supplied, leaving its methods, effect estimates and uncertainty unassessed beyond the perspective’s preliminary account.
It remains uncertain whether preventing or clearing amyloid plaques is sufficient to stop long-term clinical progression, and what treatment duration would provide durable protection.
Generalization from dominantly inherited disease to the broader sporadic at-risk population remains unestablished in the supplied evidence.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether later results changed the June 2026 account by November 1, 2026.
The proposed completion framework still requires concrete effect-size, follow-up, safety and practical-access thresholds; no numerical thresholds are established here.

brief.title: Preventing Alzheimer’s before independence is lost
possible: People at risk of Alzheimer’s could receive treatment while they still feel healthy and keep their memory, thinking and ability to manage daily life. This would require identifying who is likely to develop dementia early enough to prevent lasting loss.
why: Effective prevention would give people more years of independence. It could also reduce the demands on families and carers and the need for long-term care.

sources.who: Christopher H van Dyck and collaborators
sources.showed: Lecanemab slowed worsening of thinking and daily function over 18 months in people with early Alzheimer’s symptoms. It also reduced amyloid, a protein that forms deposits in the brain, but caused adverse effects.
sources.quote: Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events.
sources.cited_for: Treatment targeting amyloid can slow decline after symptoms begin.
sources.not_established: Slowing decline after symptoms begin does not establish prevention before symptoms or lasting protection.

sources.who: E. McDade and collaborators, DIAN-TU and DIAN-Obs
sources.showed: They describe a prevention trial platform for people with inherited Alzheimer’s risk. It measures biomarkers, biological signs of disease, to test treatment before detectable amyloid deposits develop.
sources.quote: This framework has enabled the launch of a platform trial incorporating biomarker outcomes that span successive phases of preclinical disease, allowing detection and quantification of downstream disease-modifying effects from preventing Aβ accumulation.
sources.cited_for: Trials can test early biological effects before symptoms appear.
sources.not_established: The trial design does not demonstrate that treatment prevents dementia or preserves daily function.

shown: Preliminary findings from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network suggest gantenerumab may delay first symptoms in people with a rare inherited form of Alzheimer’s. Participants knew they were receiving treatment. Durable prevention in the broader population remains unproven.
missing: Reliable early identification of people in the general population who are likely to develop Alzheimer’s dementia remains a challenge.
No treatment has demonstrated safe, durable prevention of Alzheimer’s dementia with preserved daily function.
A workable duration of preventive treatment, with acceptable long-term harms and monitoring demands, remains unknown.
An affordable route from screening to treatment and monitoring has yet to support prevention at population scale.

milestones.label: Trials show lasting prevention with acceptable safety
milestones.explanation: Large trials with randomly assigned treatment would have to reduce dementia durably, preserve daily function and meet agreed safety limits. This would establish benefit before substantial impairment.

milestones.label: People retain thinking and everyday abilities
milestones.explanation: Clinical outcomes would have to demonstrate prevention of dementia and functional loss, with biological measurements supporting the findings. This would establish that treatment protects people’s abilities.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm who benefits and for how long
milestones.explanation: Independent studies in diverse populations would have to confirm protection and whether it requires continued treatment. This would distinguish lasting benefit from temporary delay and establish its scope.

milestones.label: Prevention becomes affordable and practical at population scale
milestones.explanation: Risk screening, treatment and monitoring would have to be affordable and manageable for people without symptoms. This would make prevention usable beyond specialized trials.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether preventing or clearing amyloid deposits is enough to stop long-term decline.
Protection in rare inherited Alzheimer’s may not translate to the more common form without those mutations.
The benefit, follow-up duration and acceptable harms needed to judge prevention successful still need concrete thresholds.
